stories.title: Affiliated Closes Financing on Mixed-Income Fort Lauderdale Apartment Venture
stories.excerpt: Affiliated Development has closed on a $74 million construction loan with Pacific Life Insurance Company for The Cove, a mixed-use, mixed-income multifamily development on the northwest corner of Sunrise Boulevard and Federal Highway in Fort Lauderdale. Just over half of the 374 units will be restricted to families earning 120% of the Area Median Income. In exchange for the rent restrictions, Fort Lauderdale and Broward County offered tax rebates. The Cove will rise on the site of a former hotel property. The site was home to the Clarion Inn and The Link hotel until it was recently demolished. Moss Construction is serving as general contractor on The Cove. Rinka is the project’s architect. The project is being capitalized with a $74 million construction loan from Pacific Life Insurance Company, equity from Affiliated Housing Impact Fund, LP and family office capital partners. Construction on The Cove is expected to commence immediately following closing. The post Affiliated Closes Financing on Mixed-Income Fort Lauderdale Apartment Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Affiliated closes $74M construction loan from Pacific Life for 374-unit mixed-income Fort Lauderdale apartment.
50% of units restricted to 120% AMI; Fort Lauderdale and Broward County offer tax rebates.
Demolition of Clarion Inn and Link hotel enables mixed-use development on Sunrise Boulevard and Federal Highway.
stories.summary: Affiliated Development closed a $74 million construction loan from Pacific Life Insurance for The Cove, a 374-unit mixed-income multifamily project in Fort Lauderdale on the site of two former hotels. Over half the units are deed-restricted to families earning 120% AMI, and the developer secured tax rebates from Fort Lauderdale and Broward County in exchange. Construction is expected to commence immediately.
stories.impact: Tax incentives for mixed-income housing signal Fort Lauderdale's policy embrace of workforce rentals, reducing developer cost basis and improving returns in a high-cost South Florida submarket. The adaptive reuse of hotel land into residential reflects sustained multifamily demand in a market where office-to-residential conversions are also gaining traction; this de-risking of legacy hospitality assets opens supply opportunities.

stories.title: Olmstead Signs Luckin Coffee to 10-Year Lease in Hudson Square
stories.excerpt: Olmstead Properties has signed Luckin Coffee to a new 10-year, 1,200-square-foot retail lease at 180 Varick St., bringing one of the country’s fastest-growing coffee brands to the base of the historic Hudson Square office building. Luckin Coffee will replace a neighborhood pizzeria and deli that had occupied the storefront for more than 40 years before its longtime owner retired. Steven Marvin of Olmstead Properties represented ownership. “Luckin Coffee is an outstanding addition to 180 Varick St. and exactly the type of tenant we were seeking for the building,” said Marvin. “As Hudson Square continues to evolve as one of Manhattan’s most dynamic office neighborhoods, we’re focused on bringing in amenities that enhance the daily experience for our tenants while serving the surrounding community. Luckin has built a strong following by delivering a modern, convenient coffee experience, and we’re excited to welcome them to the building.” 180 Varick St. has been owned by the Rosenblatt family since it was developed in the 1920s by Sam Rosenblatt’s great-grandfather, making it Olmstead Properties’ longest-held asset. The post Olmstead Signs Luckin Coffee to 10-Year Lease in Hudson Square appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Luckin Coffee signs 10-year retail lease at 180 Varick Street in Hudson Square Manhattan.
1,200-square-foot ground-floor lease replaces 40-year neighborhood pizzeria and deli.
Olmstead Properties emphasizes amenities strategy to attract tenants in evolving Manhattan office submarket.
stories.summary: Olmstead Properties leased 1,200 square feet of ground-floor retail at 180 Varick Street in Hudson Square to Luckin Coffee, one of the country's fastest-growing coffee brands, on a 10-year deal. The lease replaces a long-standing neighborhood pizzeria and deli. Olmstead stated the leasing strategy reflects its focus on amenities that enhance the experience for office tenants and the surrounding community.
stories.impact: Minimal impact to multifamily development. Coffee tenant leasing signals modest office-submarket stabilization in Hudson Square but does not materially affect residential demand drivers or capital availability for apartment projects.

stories.title: Northmarq Arranges Refi for Grocery-Anchored Queens Retail
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s New York Metro Debt + Equity team led by Robert Delitsky and Keith Braddish arranged the $15-million refinance of Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center. The 34,949-square-foot, multi-tenant anchored center is located at 102-20 Atlantic Avenue in the Ozone Park section of Queens. Northmarq arranged the financing on behalf of the owner, Schuckman Realty Inc., through a relationship with a commercial bank. “We are thrilled to have arranged this financing for our long-time client on this premier retail center,” Delitsky said. “This transaction reflects the continued strength of well-located retail properties in the boroughs and Northmarq’s ability to deliver financing solutions to meet our clients’ objectives.” Added Ken Schuckman, president of Schuckman Realty, “Grocery-anchored retail in the boroughs is as strong as we’ve ever seen it — well-located neighborhood centers with daily-needs tenants are outperforming the market, and lenders know it.” Built in 1984, Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center is leased to daily-needs tenants including Bravo Supermarkets, Lenox Hill Radiology, Four Leaf Federal Credit Union and Dunkin’. The post Northmarq Arranges Refi for Grocery-Anchored Queens Retail appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Northmarq arranges $15M refinance of 34,949-square-foot grocery-anchored retail center in Ozone Park, Queens.
Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center anchored by Bravo Supermarkets, Dunkin', Lenox Hill Radiology; built 1984.
Lender appetite strong for well-located neighborhood retail with daily-needs tenants in NYC boroughs.
stories.summary: Northmarq's New York Metro team arranged a $15 million refinance for Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center, a 34,949-square-foot grocery-anchored retail property in Ozone Park, Queens, through a commercial bank relationship. The property is leased to daily-needs tenants including Bravo Supermarkets, Dunkin', and Lenox Hill Radiology. The owner noted that grocery-anchored neighborhood centers in the boroughs are performing at historic strength.
stories.impact: Minimal impact to multifamily development. Lender strength on grocery-anchored retail in outer boroughs confirms commercial real estate confidence in outer-borough submarkets but does not directly signal residential demand or capital repositioning toward apartments.

stories.title: Marcus & Millichap Closes $12.5M Sale of La Mesa Seniors Housing
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap finalized the sale of 5035-49 Guava Ave., an 81-unit seniors affordable multifamily property located in La Mesa. The property sold for $12.5 million, or $154,320 per unit. “Age-restricted communities with long-term affordability protections are rarely available for acquisition in San Diego County,” said Christopher Zorbas, executive managing director investments. “This transaction reflects the continued demand for well-maintained affordable senior housing, and despite broader industry headwinds, we remain confident in the long-term fundamentals of the La Mesa and greater San Diego rental market.” said Graeme Henderson, director of investments. “New ownership is poised to keep providing low-income senior housing for years to come, given the property is the only senior deed restricted building with an agreement in perpetuity in the submarket.” Zorbas, Henderson, and Austin Huffman, investment specialists in Marcus & Millichap’s San Diego Del Mar office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a private owner, and procured the buyer, Positive Investments, based out of Los Angeles. The sale marks one of five transactions over 80 units in La Mesa and one of seven senior affordable transactions countywide in the past five years. The marketing team conducted over 20 tours of the 1986-vintage asset and had multiple competing offers The post Marcus & Millichap Closes $12.5M Sale of La Mesa Seniors Housing appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap sells 81-unit age-restricted affordable property in La Mesa, San Diego for $12.5M ($154K/unit).
Long-term affordability protections; property built 1986; marked one of five 80+ unit transactions in La Mesa in five years.
Buyer Positive Investments (Los Angeles-based) acquiring for continued low-income senior housing operations.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the $12.5 million sale of an 81-unit age-restricted affordable multifamily property at 5035-49 Guava Avenue in La Mesa, San Diego, at $154,320 per unit. The property features long-term affordability protections and was built in 1986. Buyer Positive Investments, a Los Angeles-based firm, acquired the asset to continue providing low-income senior housing.
stories.impact: Senior affordable housing scarcity in San Diego County (one of five 80+ unit deals in La Mesa in five years) suggests limited pipeline and sustained nonprofit/impact investor demand for deed-restricted seniors communities. Pricing at $154K/unit reflects value-add or cash-flow stabilization potential in a capital-constrained affordable housing market; indicates opportunity for developers with access to below-market capital or tax credits to pursue similar acquisitions.

stories.title: NAI DiLeo-Bram Markets Piscataway Industrial in Key Supply Chain Corridor
stories.excerpt: NAI DiLeo-Bram & Co. (NAIDB) is marketing 240 Circle Drive North, a 74,500-square-foot industrial building situated on approximately five acres in Piscataway, NJ. The property features a 6,000-square-foot office component and is suited for an owner-user buyer seeking to establish or expand their strategic foothold in this Central New Jersey supply chain corridor. The marketing assignment is being led by the NAIDB brokerage team of VPs Kyle Gerace and Chris Chiusolo alongside COO David A. Simon. The team has multi-decade familiarity with the property associated with Managing Director Chris Galiano’s involvement in past leasing transactions. Positioned within the Piscataway industrial hub, the property is easily accessible via two separate I-287 interchanges, which directly connect with the New Jersey Turnpike, Garden State Parkway, Routes 1, 18, 22, I-78 and I-80. “Opportunities of this size for user-buyers are exceedingly rare in today’s market, especially within land-constrained infill corridors,” said Gerace. “Based on the current market cycle, 240 Circle Drive North delivers the exact combination of heavy power, functional logistics infrastructure and strategic regional connectivity that modern operators require to insulate and scale their businesses.”  The post NAI DiLeo-Bram Markets Piscataway Industrial in Key Supply Chain Corridor appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NAI DiLeo-Bram markets 74,500-square-foot industrial building in Piscataway, NJ on five acres.
Property features 6,000-square-foot office component; positioned for owner-user in Central Jersey supply chain corridor.

stories.summary: NAI DiLeo-Bram is marketing 240 Circle Drive North, a 74,500-square-foot industrial building on five acres in Piscataway, NJ, featuring a 6,000-square-foot office component. The property is positioned for owner-users seeking to establish or expand operations within the Central New Jersey supply chain corridor. The site enjoys multi-highway accessibility via two I-287 interchanges connecting to the New Jersey Turnpike, Garden State Parkway, and major state routes.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development. Industrial owner-user marketing in Central Jersey reflects continued logistics infrastructure investment but does not signal residential demand migration or housing supply constraints that would benefit apartment development.

stories.title: Peachtree Lends $113M on Apartments’ Conversion to Margaritaville Hotel Savannah
stories.excerpt: Tidal Real Estate Partners is “waving” hello to the opportunity to convert a Savannah, Ga., multifamily building into a Margaritaville-branded hotel. The New York City development firm just sealed $113 million of bridge debt to recapitalize and repurpose the 2023-built Ann Street Lofts property into the 230-key Margaritaville Hotel Savannah, Commercial Observer has learned Peachtree Group originated the three-year floating-rate loan with two 12-month extension options for the multifamily-to-hospitality conversion project in Downtown Savannah. The conversion project is slated to commence late this summer. Jared Schlosser, head of credit originations at Peachtree Group, said after developing Ann Street Lofts as Georgia’s first large-scale mass timber multifamily project, Tidal opted to pivot the 232-unit property to hotel use after evaluating market conditions. Schlosser noted that the property is positioned for success given Savannah’s strong tourism numbers, with more than 18 million annual visitors coupled with a limited lodging supply within the city’s Historic District. “There’s a lot of development happening in this immediate area and a lot of planned development happening in this immediate area,” Schlosser told Commercial Observer. “The market continues to have a big influx of tourism and conferences so there is a good mix of demand drivers.” Walker & Dunlop negotiated the debt with a team led by Michael Brown and Keith Kurland. The Margaritaville Hotel Savannah is slated to debut in summer 2027. It will include a hotel pool deck, a Jimmy Buffett’s Margaritaville restaurant concept, and a LandShark Bar & Grill. Schlosser said the hotel will be designed for both leisure travelers as well as local residents seeking food, beverage and resort-style amenities. bullets: Peachtree Group originates $113M bridge financing for multifamily-to-hospitality conversion in Savannah, Georgia.

The three-year floating-rate loan features two 12-month extension options. Conversion work is scheduled to commence in late summer, driven by Savannah's strong tourism fundamentals (18+ million annual visitors).
stories.impact: Multifamily-to-hospitality conversion reflects asset-level demand volatility; developer pivot from residential to hotel use signals either (1) softer rental absorption than originally modeled, or (2) higher-yield hospitality opportunity in a tourism-driven market. The reliance on bridge financing with floating rates exposes the deal to rising SOFR; if conversion yields disappoint, could signal caution around residential development in secondary markets like Savannah facing tourism competition for capital and land use.

stories.title: AI Is Rewiring the Office-Leasing Playbook
stories.excerpt: Much of the conversation around artificial intelligence and commercial real estate leasing has focused on whether AI will bring people back to the office. I think that’s the wrong question. The more important one is where AI companies are choosing to invest, hire and build because those decisions tell us far more about the next office cycle than return-to-office policies. After 20 years in commercial real estate, I’ve learned to be skeptical of bold predictions. I’ve watched plenty of cycles get oversold, but this one feels different, and the data tells us why. Start with where demand is actually concentrating. One submarket in San Francisco — the non-core central business district, including South of Market and Mission Bay — is responsible for 25 percent of all active AI office demand across the markets we track. San Francisco’s South Financial District accounts for another 16 percent, San Jose another 14 percent, and New York City’s Midtown South and Midtown another 11 percent and 8 percent, respectively. Ryan Masiello. These five submarkets across three markets account for nearly three-quarters of current AI square footage. National AI office demand is up 85 percent year-over-year, but, across the industry’s largest AI hubs, demand is up 179 percent. The story isn’t simply growth — it’s concentrated growth. Today’s market is fundamentally different from the last tech cycle. OpenAI raised $122 billion in February at an $840 billion valuation. Anthropic followed with $30 billion in a Series G at $380 billion. These aren’t 2022-era companies burning headcount against speculative valuations — both are scaling revenue far faster than headcount. Not only are current fundamentals far more sound, but the market opportunity is massive. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently stated that writing code is not the job of a software engineer. bullets: AI company office demand concentrated in five submarkets: SF SOMA/Mission Bay (25%), SF South Financial (16%), San Jose (14%), NYC Midtown South (11%), NYC Midtown (8%).
These five submarkets account for nearly 75% of tracked active AI office demand across three markets.
AI hiring patterns, not return-to-office mandates, drive next office cycle and regional concentration.
stories.summary: A commercial real estate analyst reports that AI company office demand is highly concentrated geographically. San Francisco's South of Market/Mission Bay alone accounts for 25% of all tracked AI office demand; San Francisco's South Financial District adds 16%, San Jose 14%, and NYC's Midtown South and Midtown contribute 11% and 8%, respectively. These five submarkets across three metros capture nearly 75% of active AI office demand, suggesting that AI hiring decisions, not broad return-to-office trends, are reshaping the office market.
stories.impact: AI-driven office clustering in SOMA, South Financial, Midtown South, and San Jose signals sustained demand for premium, spec-free office space in tech-forward submarkets. This concentration raises rents and capital values in those neighborhoods, pricing out older office stock and potentially spurring adaptive reuse of secondary office to residential. Multifamily developers should monitor AI talent migration into these tech hubs (and their residential peripheries) for rental demand tailwinds, but should avoid direct competition with office in core AI districts.

stories.title: Legal AI Firm Sandstone Signs 14K-SF Lease at 141 East Houston Street
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-powered management platform designed to help law firms has signed an office lease on the Lower East Side, Commercial Observer has learned. AI platform Sandstone signed a five-year deal spanning 13,794 square feet on the entire third and fourth floors of East End Capital’s 141 East Houston Street, according to landlord broker Current Real Estate Advisors. Asking rent for the space was $93 per square foot. “This transaction is another example of what we’re continuing to see across the market,” Current’s Adam Henick, who represented the landlord alongside Rob Kluge, said in a statement. “We believed early on that delivering a newly built, fully furnished space with a premium level of finish would give the building a real competitive advantage, and this lease validates that strategy. When landlords invest in creating a best-in-class product, the market continues to reward it.” Newmark represented the tenant, which is relocating from 45 Main Street in Brooklyn, but the brokerage did not immediately respond to a request for comment. East End Capital developed the 63,000-square-foot property between Forsyth and Eldridge streets with Grandview Partners and Greg Kraut’s KPG Funds between 2020 and 2022 with designs by Roger Ferris + Partners. At the time, the project signaled a different kind of development pattern in the trendy enclave. Built on the site of the historic Sunshine Cinema, it’s unclear where the building stands in terms of occupancy, but it was around 50 percent full when the owners refinanced the property with a $79.6 million from Fortress in 2022. That same year, a private dining club that sold memberships through non-fungible tokens (remember those?) known as the Flyfish Club signed an 11,000-square-foot lease for three stories in the building. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Legal AI platform Sandstone signs five-year lease for 13,794 square feet on floors 3-4 of 141 East Houston Street, Lower East Side Manhattan.
Tenant relocating from 45 Main Street, Brooklyn; lease reflects landlord investment in newly built, fully furnished, premium-finish space.
Current Real Estate Advisors notes market continues to reward landlords investing in best-in-class office product.
stories.summary: Sandstone, an AI-powered management platform for law firms, signed a five-year lease spanning the entire third and fourth floors (13,794 square feet) of 141 East Houston Street on the Lower East Side, Manhattan. The tenant relocated from Brooklyn office space. The landlord, East End Capital, had invested in newly constructed, fully furnished, and premium-finish office, a strategy the leasing broker said the market rewards.
stories.impact: Minimal impact to multifamily development. AI legal-tech company leasing in Lower East Side signals office recovery in a secondary Manhattan submarket but does not materially shift residential demand or capital allocation toward apartments. However, tech-sector relocation into residential-mixed neighborhoods may incrementally boost local amenity demand and foot traffic, benefiting nearby residential projects through indirect network effects.

stories.title: Grun Group Files Plans for Pair of 99-Unit Residential Buildings in the Bronx
stories.excerpt: Real estate investment and development firm Grun Group has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) to bring a pair of 99-unit residential towers to the Bronx’s Woodlawn Heights neighborhood, records show. If approved, the first of the two new buildings will be at 4241 Webster Avenue and span 59,611 square feet. This development will have 99 units across eight floors. The second building will be in the same neighborhood at 4230 Peters Place, spanning 68,733 square feet and also with 99 units. The properties are currently both parking lots. The DOB plans do not provide much more information. Grun Group did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Developers have been busy in the Bronx as of late. Catholic Homes, an affiliate of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of New York, recently secured $146.9 million in construction financing to build affordable housing at 484 East 178th Street in the Bronx. Meanwhile, the city closed on $214 million in financing to bring 288 affordable senior units to 3728 Park Avenue, while housing developer Vilson Lumaj is planning two 99-unit residential properties at 761-769 East Tremont Avenue. Grun Group itself has lately been working on several projects in the city. In Kew Gardens, Queens, Grun Group filed plans in June to build a nine-story, 108-unit residential building at 116-18 Grosnevor Lane. And in January, the firm submitted an application to construct a 94-unit apartment building at 469 Troy Avenue in East Flatbush, Brooklyn. Though unconfirmed, it is probable that Grun opted to build two 99-unit residentials at its new project in Woodlawn Heights as a way to take advantage of the city’s 485-x tax abatement program. Limiting the size of a project allows developers to reap the tax benefits of 485-x without paying the high construction wages required when building 100 or more units. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Grun Group files plans for two 99-unit residential towers in Woodlawn Heights, Bronx (Webster Avenue and Peters Place).
Buildings span 59,611 and 68,733 square feet, respectively; developments on current parking lots.
Catholic Homes, city, and other developers actively pursuing Bronx residential; Catholic Homes secured $146.9M construction financing for affordable housing.
stories.summary: Grun Group filed development plans with NYC Department of Buildings for two 99-unit residential towers in the Bronx's Woodlawn Heights neighborhood: one at 4241 Webster Avenue (59,611 square feet) and one at 4230 Peters Place (68,733 square feet). Both properties currently operate as parking lots. The news reflects a broader wave of residential development in the Bronx, including Catholic Homes' recent $146.9 million construction financing for affordable housing at 178th Street.
stories.impact: Grun Group's two-tower pipeline in Woodlawn Heights signals developer confidence in Bronx rental fundamentals and land assembly feasibility. The adjacent wave of affordable housing and senior development (Catholic Homes, city-financed projects) suggests municipality support and subsidy availability. Developers should monitor Bronx neighborhood infrastructure (transit, schools, amenities) and zoning flexibility as entitlement barriers in outer boroughs remain lower than Manhattan, favoring project velocity and underwriting stability.

stories.title: Dedeaux Properties CEO Brett Dedeaux On SoCal’s Evergreen Industrial Pull
stories.excerpt: For Dedeaux Properties, California’s infamously arduous development environment can be both a hurdle and a competitive advantage. CEO Brett Dedeaux spoke with Commercial Observer about why the firm sees Tejon Ranch as such a compelling alternative to Los Angeles County and the Inland Empire, as well as how the state’s regulations can add value to entitlements, and why the company remains committed to its home turf. The following is the second of a two-part conversation, and has been edited for length and clarity. Click here for the first part. Commercial Observer: Tejon Ranch is rapidly expanding as an alternative logistics location. When did you start looking that far north? The construction site of the new plant. Photo by Frank Hammerschmidt/picture alliance via Getty Images Brett Dedeaux: A couple of years back, we bought land from Tejon Ranch and built about 230,000 square feet with excess trailer parking. That performed well, and we sold it to an owner-user in 2024, and that led to a broader joint venture with Tejon Ranch to build out more industrial space. Labor is a big part of the appeal for any logistics company. There is affordable labor and more affordable housing in Tejon Ranch. We kind of say, “Tejon Ranch is the Texas of California.” It is a very business-friendly environment where things get done relatively quickly. It is not as overly regulated. For big-box deals, if you have to go farther and farther east to Beaumont, Banning or the High Desert, Tejon Ranch is a competitive alternative from a drayage and transportation cost standpoint. You can easily get back into the L.A. Basin, but you can also service Northern California and the Western and Northwestern U.S. We also have plentiful power at Tejon Ranch, which is really key. Then look at the San Fernando Valley. If it seceded from the City of Los Angeles, I believe it would be one of the largest cities in the country. It has a large population base, a big manufacturing base, a lot of aerospace and
bullets: Dedeaux Properties CEO highlights Tejon Ranch (north of Los Angeles) as compelling alternative to LA County and Inland Empire logistics development.
Labor cost and affordable housing availability drive owner-user and logistics tenant attraction to Tejon Ranch submarket.
Dedeaux sold 230,000-square-foot industrial asset to owner-user in 2024; now pursuing broader joint venture with Tejon Ranch for additional industrial build-out.
stories.summary: Dedeaux Properties CEO Brett Dedeaux discusses Tejon Ranch's emergence as a logistics and industrial alternative to Los Angeles County and the Inland Empire, driven by lower labor costs and more affordable housing. The firm purchased land from Tejon Ranch, developed 230,000 square feet with excess trailer parking (sold to an owner-user in 2024), and is now expanding a broader joint venture with Tejon Ranch for additional industrial expansion.
stories.impact: Tejon Ranch's growing appeal as an owner-user and logistics destination reflects supply constraints and rising land/labor costs in LA County and Inland Empire; this geographic shift signals tightening industrial capacity closer to Los Angeles, potentially supporting infill multifamily near Port of LA, Inland Empire, and traditional logistics corridors. However, Tejon Ranch's industrial pull may also siphon logistics employers and their associated workforce housing demand away from regional multifamily markets, requiring developers to evaluate long-term labor migration patterns and rent growth sustainability in traditional Southern California apartment submarkets.
